what_its_for: Mercaptopurine is used to treat a type of blood cancer called acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). It works by slowing down or stopping the growth of cancer cells in your body. It is also sometimes used to treat inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.
how_to_take: Take mercaptopurine exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. It is best to take it on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after eating, because food can reduce how well your body absorbs it. Try to take it at the same time every day. If you are using the liquid form (Purixan), shake the bottle well before each use and measure your dose carefully with the special measuring device provided — do not use a regular kitchen spoon.
dosing: Your dose is based on your body weight, body surface area, and your specific condition. Your doctor will calculate the right dose for you. Do not change your dose on your own. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on blood test results or side effects you experience. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular scheduled time. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for advice.
storage: Store mercaptopurine tablets at room temperature, away from heat, light, and moisture. Keep the bottle tightly closed. Store the liquid form (Purixan) in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze the liquid. Keep all forms of this medication out of reach of children and pets. Throw away any unused liquid after 6 weeks of opening the bottle.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking mercaptopurine with food, especially dairy products or high-fat meals, as they can lower the amount of drug your body absorbs. Do not take allopurinol (a gout medication) unless your doctor is aware, as it can cause dangerous levels of mercaptopurine in your blood. Avoid live vaccines (such as the flu nasal spray or chickenpox vaccine) while on this medication. Avoid contact with people who are sick, as this drug can weaken your immune system and make you more likely to get infections. Limit alcohol, as it can increase the risk of liver problems. Tell your doctor about ALL other medications, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: fever, chills, or signs of infection (such as sore throat or burning when urinating); unusual bruising or bleeding; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); dark-colored urine or pale stools; severe nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain; mouth sores that are severe or preventing you from eating or drinking; extreme tiredness or weakness; shortness of breath; or any new or worsening symptoms. Also contact your doctor if you think you may be pregnant while taking this medication.
when_it_works: Mercaptopurine does not work overnight. For leukemia, it is part of a long-term treatment plan that may take months to years. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular blood tests. You may not feel any different right away, but the medication is working in the background to fight cancer cells. It is very important to keep taking it even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Mercaptopurine can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment. Do not breastfeed while taking this medication. Talk to your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Children: This drug is commonly used in children with ALL and is dosed carefully based on body size. Children should be closely monitored by their healthcare team. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects, especially bone marrow suppression, and may need closer monitoring. Kidney or liver problems: If you have kidney or liver disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose, as the drug is processed by the liver and kidneys. Genetic testing: Some people have a gene variation (TPMT or NUDT15 deficiency) that makes them break down this drug more slowly, increasing the risk of serious side effects. Your doctor may test for this before starting treatment.
